Social distancing implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions in major cities worldwide. This research analyzes data on 25 million anonymized mobile phone users in five diverse countries to explore the impact of these reduced interactions on socioeconomic inequality. By comparing the pre-pandemic period with the initial pandemic period, our findings indicate that the lowest 50% of users with regards to daily face-to-face interactions saw a 23% decline in their existing limitations, whereas the top 10% of users experienced only a 3% decrease in their interactions. Consequently, the gap between these users widened by 20%. When adjusting for various factors including age, gender, location, and financial status, our data reveal that the low-mid economic class showed the greatest decline (37%) in urban interactions, whereas high-income citizens experienced a relatively mild reduction (4%) of the same order. These results suggest that deliberate behavioral changes caused by the pandemic have exacerbated income-based disparities in urban interactions, limiting the potential for long-term social and economic development.

The process of massive star formation remains poorly understood due to the relatively short times before massive protostars turn into luminous young stars, making observations during this period rare and challenging. Despite this difficulty, researchers were able to identify 13.4 mm continuum clusters within a massive protostar cluster called IRAS 00965, providing insights into the formation and collision of small solid particles in the vicinity of this protostar. By analyzing these observations along with existing data from other wavelengths, a comprehensive picture of the area has been revealed, spanning the outer reaches of a molecular disk that surrounds the protostar and extends over 100 AU in all directions. Evidence of both rapid accretion and the ejection of high-speed jets was also found, suggesting that the collapse of this particular protostar is not a steady process but rather dynamic, with material accreting at remarkable rates of up to 10^-4 per year. Furthermore, collisions between solid particles have been identified at the inner edges of the disk, where they transfer considerable amounts of mass and momentum, potentially disrupting the accretion process and diverting material back into the protostar, and may also lead to the formation of small dust clumps that eventually become planitary embryos.

This research develops a Hamiltonian formulation of the Dysthe equation, which describes how deep-water gravity waves interact with water of uniform depth and vorticity, given that the amplitude of these waves is relatively small compared to their wavelength and the width of their spectrum. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation includes a new term involving the square of the water's vorticity and is necessary to maintain the Hamiltonian property of the equation. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation can be linearized to the Hamiltonian version of the KdV equation, as well as the Hamiltonian version of the Dysthe equation for surface gravity waves without vorticity. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation can be obtained from a Hamiltonian formulation of the deep-water gravity wave equation that uses a variational principle based on a precise variation of the action, which can be achieved through a transformation of the potential vorticity. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation can also be derived from a Hamiltonian formulation of the deep-water gravity wave equation that uses a variational principle based on a precise variation of the action, which can be achieved through a transformation of the water depth, leading to the Hamiltonian KdV equation.

This research paper introduces differential forms and differential operators on a class of generalized manifold concepts, which it calls locally arching spaces. It demonstrates the necessity of employing differential operators in proving a generalized Stokes theorem. Additionally, it explores the relationship between these operator definitions and commutative diagrams of differential forms.

Autonomous navigation in complex indoor environments with low-ceiling spaces and temperature gradients is a challenging task for mobile robots. To achieve full control, multiple sensors must be seamlessly integrated in real-time, presenting a significant programming complexity. This project aimed to simplify robot navigation by developing a straightforward protocol for simultaneous sonar and temperature sensor usage. A basic C++ program was created to manage sensor data in real-time, providing access to sensor values, maximum/minimum temperatures, and gradient calculations. The program was tested on a robot equipped with sonar sensors and temperature probes placed at different heights, accurately detecting the robot's position, detecting temperature gradients, and alerting the operator with auditory signals.

The veracity of information is a critical aspect in today's social media environment, and false news spread quickly. To combat this issue, it's essential to develop techniques for accurately identifying the truth-content of information. In this paper, an advanced method is introduced that combines topic modeling and neural networks to determine the truth-content of information. Specifically, a dense topic model is proposed to organize and simplify information based on a proposed metric called the Relative Specificity (RS), which facilitates the development of a trained neural network model that can accurately identify the truth-content of information. The proposed method was evaluated and compared to existing techniques, revealing its superior performance in false news detection and content truth assessment.

This research paper examines how geometric properties, specifically curvature, influence Gaussian stochastic fields. It discovers a distinct class of stochastic fields determined by their curvature, which can be viewed as a key aspect of their topological nature. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for fields with a specific type of curvature, namely those with a certain H\"older character, the probability of a sample having a certain property decreases in line with its curvature in specific instances. It is also shown that fields with certain fractal characteristics can be incorporated into this framework. It is noted that existing research already addresses fields with curved boundaries.

This work presents a novel iterative method for computing the principal component associated with the $\ell_1$-norm loss function, particularly in the context where data points exhibit rotational symmetry. We demonstrate that our approach converges linearly to the desired component, and this convergence is ensured through a new tail bound that reflects the algorithm's performance and its dependence on various relevant factors. To establish and use the bound mentioned above, we apply a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling technique and a particular random walk model that leads to a combinatorial process, specifically U(V,t), which involves swapping edges in a graph, and this process has a known relationship with the eigenvalue of interest, allowing us to apply the method with an appropriate period length. It is worthwhile to note that our approach and the associated theory can be applied to a more general class of loss functions that include the $\ell_1$-norm loss function as a special case.

Understanding the emotional content of language is crucial for addressing the complexities of human emotion, which is a fundamental aspect of natural language.  Natural language processing models have achieved significant success in tasks like sentiment analysis and emotion recognition, yet there's still a lack of knowledge regarding the subtle connections between these emotions in question sentences.  This work focuses on expanding the emotion-based tagging system to account for the intricate relationships between emotions in question sentences, using a dataset carefully selected for this purpose.  A novel semantic tagging adjustment method is proposed, which incorporates a subtle connection between emotions as a key tagging criterion.  The proposed method was implemented and evaluated on the designated dataset, showing significant improvements over existing methods.

For robots to effectively navigate complex, previously unseen environments, they need to be able to construct detailed maps that accurately reflect the space's layout. In many real-world applications, having access to exact distance measurements is not always necessary, thanks to the development of sampling-based navigation methods that utilize probability fields to represent an environment. Our novel HiTMap framework builds upon these methods while incorporating a new hierarchical structure that enables efficient navigation by focusing on the overall layout and eliminating the need for precise measurement of individual distances. Through simulation and real-world testing, HiTMap demonstrates substantial gains in navigation speed and efficiency, proving that a hierarchical representation can be a superior alternative to traditional mapping approaches in situations where measurement accuracy is uncertain.

One of the most sensitive methods for detecting changes in position is atomic interferometry. By converting a position variation into a phase shift within an atomic interference pattern, this method can identify even tiny changes in distance. We suggest a novel atomic interferometry technique that can accurately measure the effect of magnetic fields on matter, specifically the Meissner effect exhibited by superconducting materials. When a superconductor is placed near atomic particles creating an interference pattern, the response to the generated magnetic field due to the Meissner effect will result in a detectable shift in the atomic distribution. This technique can detect the minimal amount of superconducting material required to realize the Meissner effect and identify tiny changes in the superconducting state induced by external fields, providing valuable information about the effect of magnetic fields on matter.

This research introduces a novel interpretation of finite mixture models, reclassifying them as models that incorporate spatial variations and structural changes. A new algorithm is developed to handle changes in structure and is based on geometric methods to define regions associated with unknown parameters. The algorithm identifies areas associated with point processes representing the underlying data, and it detects areas associated with parameter combinations that match real data patterns. The research further demonstrates that finite mixture models are a special case of models that account for variations in data and are therefore equivalent to models that account for changes in structure, making them models that incorporate spatial variations and structural changes. The research also explores the relationship with classical finite mixture models, offering a novel interpretation of their parameters.

Due to the intricate nature of memory management and memory access, programming modern CPUs with direct access to memory can be complicated.  As a result, programmers prefer using object-based programming techniques that simplify memory management by allocating memory through objects rather than raw memory addresses.  Although object-based programming in CPU programming has numerous advantages, there is a lack of research in this area for programming on GPUs.  In fact, most GPU programming uses flat memory addressing to enhance performance and simplify memory management.  This work introduces DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed especially for object-based programming on certain GPUs.  DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization, reduces fragmentation, and matches the raw speed of current GPU fast memory allocators.  This processor also includes a block of registers that may be used for small data objects, including structures of up to 64 bytes without the need for additional memory allocation.  This research was part of the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute's Topic 2: Advanced Computing with NVIDIA GPUs project.

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to describe the spin polarization of superconducting states in the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) category, based on initial principles. This approach, which incorporates a controllable parameter to represent the extent of superconducting suppression, has been applied to both an individual Mn adatom and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. Calculations of magnetic moments and the spin polarization of YSR states were performed and compared with experimental results, showcasing excellent agreement. Additionally, our analysis identifies key phenomena influencing YSR states, including the interplay between their formation and the destruction of the superconducting state, and demonstrates distinctive spatial distributions of YSR states for different projections of spin polarization.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years based on spectral analysis and rotation rate. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. A fourth smaller planet with a short orbital period of $3.378$ days was also found, and it's suspected that this small planet might be an exo-Earth. Valuing the orbital eccentricity at less than $0.065$, we found the planets' masses by applying Kepler's third law and inquiring about the eccentricities, concluding that the inner planets stimulate the tidal acceleration inside the radius up to at least $10 times" more than Earth. Additionally, the investigation revealed that the system contains at least three Earth masses of atmospheric loss, suggesting that the planets lost significant amounts of gas due to tidal interactions, and it's possible that TOI-712 still possesses several small, un detected Earth-sized planets.

This study uses hybrid DFT calculations to explore the magnetic and electronic properties of carbon and nitrogen defect pairs in rutile TiO2. By examining various arrangements of these defects, we identified a favorable configuration where a N atom bonds with a C-defect in a bridge position, resulting in a spin polarized band structure and a magnetic moment of 1.62 muB. This arrangement also exhibits a significant red-shift (about 1.5 eV) in the O 2p bond energy, indicating possible influence on charge carrier transport within TiO2. This particular arrangement can be interpreted as a superparamagnetic phase that has never been observed in previous studies, and our findings suggest it may be accountable for inherent magneto-optical phenomena in TiO2.

To enhance the identification of top-quark production at the Large Hadron Colliders, we suggest implementing an analysis of forward neutron production in proton-proton collisions. Given the significant momentum carried by neutrons, they are capable of detecting high-energy elastic scattering of top quarks, a significant process despite being suppressed due to elastic scattering requirements. By combining data from existing and potential sensors, including zero-degree neutron detectors and the Forward Calorimeter at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, we propose a multifaceted approach to identify this signal. Our research indicates that identifying elastic top-quark production is feasible with existing data at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, we anticipate a significant increase in measurable events, particularly with the addition of the Forward Calorimeter which will enable the measurement of elastic top-quark production across a broader range of rapidity values.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered the study of topological Ramsey theory for graphs, leading to a sequence of groundbreaking results in both combinatorics and topology. A key problem left unresolved involves determining the Ramsey number associated with an infinite graph containing a specific component, until now specifically a double star. We achieve a significant advancement by providing a particular large estimate for this type of Ramsey number, thereby expanding our understanding of the infinite family first identified by Erdos and Galvin.

We investigate quantum electrodynamics in (1+1)D space-time, specifically the massless scalar QED model, using qutrits in combined subspace, which allows for an increase in simulated particle masses and coupling constants while maintaining the consistency of physical results. Unlike combined subspace simulations using qubits, there are no artificial constraints on the gauge field population. However, we find that in vacuum simulations, a specific set of qutrit parameter configurations can lead to unwanted beat notes in operator expectations, which may limit the achievable accuracy. Still, our results show that in matter-filled simulations, such as the example of a scalar field traversing a constant electric field, the method provides accurate mass and coupling constant calculations, even with qutrits.

Research indicates that positrons emitted at an angle of 45 degrees from a thin polarized foil target, illuminated with an intense laser and in the limit of pair production dominance, exhibit polarization properties. However, the extent to which this effect scales with target thickness remains unknown. Using an quantum electrodynamics matrix element approach and simulating intense laser-field interactions, our findings show that the positron polarization does not significantly change with increasing target thickness, a result that is independent of the target's charge density. Moreover, as thickness increases above a certain point, the polarization becomes less effective due to interference between forward-scattered photons. Additionally, the energy spectrum of the positrons exhibits a power-law dependence on the target thickness. Our predicted values are in agreement with experimental measurements made by other groups, such as the "thickness scan" experiment that utilized a gold foil.

In the context of circuit complexity, a class of functions known as total functions that can be computed by a circuit with a limited number of gates have been studied and proven to require a specific number of gates to accurately replicate the function through a specific approach. Building on the work of Bshouty and Racicot, it was demonstrated that any circuit incorporating a specific type of gate will necessarily require a particular number of gates to accurately replicate a specific type of function. Furthermore, it was also shown that there are functions that can be computed using a circuit with a limited number of gates of a particular type, and in fact, it was demonstrated that there exist functions that can be computed using a circuit with a limited number of gates of a particular type that necessitate an infinitely large number of gates of another type.

This research develops a miniature temperature detection module that integrates a bandgap reference circuit, an amplifier, and a digital temperature detection algorithm. The circuit is capable of operating across a wide voltage range of 1.8V and features low power consumption. With a precision of 0.24 degrees Celsius and an error of 1.4 degrees Celsius, this temperature detection module offers high accuracy. Furthermore, with a consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion, it outperforms existing solutions.

We introduce the concept of geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, defining them as functors from a parameter space to the category of Lie groupoids and natural transformations. These configurations possess natural symmetry groups associated with them, resulting in geometric structures on the groupoid of equivariant natural transformations when the parameter space has symmetry. Specifically, we show that certain subgroups of the automorphism group of a stack induce associated geometric structures, specifically Lie groupoids associated with the stack, with morphisms given by equivariant natural transformations.

A fascinating infrared dark complex, dubbed DRSC, has been discovered in the constellation of Draco, comprising not one but three distinct infrared dark nebulae, all sharing a common molecular core. This core, with a mass of approximately 50 solar masses, exhibits no sign of star formation, leading the authors to suggest it's undergoing a process of collapse. By analyzing the motion of a nearby water vapor stream, it was determined that the core is growing in size at a rate of about 0.2 km/s, or 600 AU per year, a remarkable rate that may be comparable to the rate of core expansion observed by Bally et al.. Furthermore, the authors find that the core's growth is driving it to collapse, leading to the formation of a dense, star-forming core at its center. Follow-up observations with the VLA and the IRAM 30m telescope revealed the presence of a massive protostar or young massive star that's still embedded within the dense core, suggesting that massive star formation may ultimately result from this process.

We establish one-step relation criteria for the consistency of stochastic field estimators under stationary, isotropic, and Gaussian assumptions, using a single observation. These criteria take into account an underlying distance between locations on the Earth's surface. We show that there exist local maxima of the likelihood function that achieve optimal one-step relation performance, and these optimal estimators are consistent when the data are normally distributed. When the data are not normally distributed, we cannot guarantee the existence of maximum likelihood estimators, but we demonstrate that the optimal one-step relation performance can be achieved by other methods, and this optimal performance is closely related to the mutual information between the data at different locations. We also provide empirical studies to compare the effectiveness of different estimators under various scenarios.

The flow of complex liquids through narrow passages is influenced by surface roughness and can lead to significant resistance, an important factor in controlling the flow of fluids in various applications, including those with surface flaws. This study delves into the resistance experienced by liquid foams as they flow through different types of surfaces, ranging from smooth to highly irregular. By examining the relationship between surface tension and the dimensionality of the foam's structure, our findings illustrate that foams exhibit high resistance in three-dimensional configurations when surface tension is low in comparison to the size of the pores. However, in two-dimensional configurations, resistance is primarily determined by the shape of the interface and is independent of surface tension. Furthermore, our data reveals that the contact angle between the interface and the surface affects the curvature of the interface and, in turn, influences resistance. In many instances, a critical contact angle exists above which the interface's curvature becomes insufficient to overcome resistance, leading to clogging. Our research demonstrates that the curvature of the interface can change in response to changes in surface tension, providing a key insight into the flow of complex liquids through narrow passages.

This study involves developing a 3D CNN model to distinguish between skin carcinomas and normal skin tissue. To ensure reliable and generalizable performance, we implemented data augmentation using geometric transformations and scattering transformations to reduce the dimensionality of features. Scattering transformations not only facilitate efficient training but also inherently develop a robustness to small outliers in the data. To extract important features from the augmented data, we employed a automatic process using a deep learning technique, specifically a dense connection network. This was done to optimize a new loss function that penalizes the model for inaccurately classifying outlier samples. As a result, the model demonstrates improved performance on unfamiliar samples similar to newly encountered test samples.

During a fluid injection into a rotating layer of another fluid, subject to restrictions at their common boundary, the shape of the interface is determined by balance equations reflecting steady state conditions, in combination with a Helmholtz-like decomposition that accounts for centrifugal force and tension within the interface. As the spinning rate is increased, multiple asymmetrical "fingering" patterns emerge that we've found to be stabilized by an increase in the depth of the outer fluid, as well as in the surface tension of that same fluid. Furthermore, in both cases where the inner fluid is forced to adhere to one boundary or not, the following conditions must be met for pattern preservation: the fluid inside must be able to move freely throughout the space, and the interface with the outer fluid must be curved in a particular way. Despite sharing some characteristics with other pattern-preserving situations, this scenario exhibits unique characteristics, particularly when the inside fluid is stuck to one boundary, that set it apart from those instances.

Scientists have detected the presence of two specific ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, CCH and CN variants of cyclopentadiene, originating from the TMC-1 direction, with estimated column densities of 1.0x10^11 molecules/cm^2 for ethynyl cyclopentadiene and 0.8x10^11 molecules/cm^2 for both isomers combined. This detection allows for a more accurate assessment of the abundance of these particular molecules, with an estimated ratio of 0.8:1 for the CCH and CN forms respectively. Furthermore, the observed emission from these molecules is concentrated within a narrow 2.5 K bandwidth, indicating a distinct temperature characteristic, with an estimated kinetic temperature of 6.7 K. This temperature data, combined with the lack of detected carbon monoxide emission, suggests that the molecules are primarily situated in a solid or liquid state. This discovery also provides the first observed evidence of cyclopentadiene, a specific hydrocarbon cycle, in the interstellar medium.

In Neural Machine Translation, the focus creation model plays a crucial role in determining which elements of the input to translate into English, but it has primarily been treated as a binary decision with recent methods using the probability of translating a token as a continuous measure. Utilizing this continuous approach, we developed a neural machine translation model that incorporates a focus creation mechanism to predict the probability of translating each input token. This model was incorporated into an attention-free neural machine translation architecture, and through experimental evaluation on multiple translation tasks, it was found that this model consistently matches the performance of state-of-the-art models utilizing complex attention mechanisms, and even surpasses them in cases where certain words are prohibited from being translated.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was hinderly dependent on tackling significant technical challenges arising from attempting to integrate disparate computer systems. Despite achieving notable success, research in grid computing became increasingly isolated from practical applications and everyday technology. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the field's focus on innovative technologies and pioneering projects, rather than developing existing concepts. We argue that this limitation contributed to the field's decline in popularity. To counter this trend, a new approach to developing grid computing was proposed, emphasizing connections between abstract theories and real-world problems. This method, known as the "translation" approach, involves rephrasing complex concepts into simpler terms and incorporating everyday examples to enhance comprehension. We applied this approach to redevelop key grid computing concepts, including workflow management, resource allocation, and security. Our results demonstrate that despite advances in grid computing, there is still value in revisiting established knowledge, and the "translation" approach can be a valuable tool for doing so.

In this work, we introduce the Dark Substantive Combined Model, a new cosmological theory that combines the dissipative dark energy and modified gravity aspects, thereby overcoming some limitations of existing models. The model, which involves a single parameter, is designed to mimic the pre-acceleration era, and we develop a straightforward method to calculate the growth factor for the model's relevant stages. Through the model's implementation in the background and perturbation phases, we determine the cosmological parameters that influence the scale-invariant regime. The model is then tested against the Hubble data and the baryon acoustic oscillation signal, and we find that it can accurately replicate the observed oscillation patterns. The model also displays the characteristic $k\approx 0.03$ oscillation behavior in the matter power spectrum. The parameter estimation yields the following results: the Hubble constant is estimated to be $67.9\pm 1.9$, the matter density parameter is $\Omega_m = 0.295\pm 0.021$, the vacuum density parameter is $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.705\pm 0.021$, the combined dark matter and dark energy density parameter is $\Omega_{rc} = 0.090\pm 0.021$, and the perturbation parameter is $2\delta-3 = 0.03\pm 0.06$. Using an effective field approach, we have investigated the implications of the J/ψ → (γ + neutrino or dark photon) invisible decays on light neutrinos and the dark energy component. We have established criteria for valid effective field theories and demonstrated that the invisible decay width of J/ψ holds significant importance in distinguishing these theories. Furthermore, we have derived consequences for the existing and future experiments in the context of neutrino and dark energy efficient field theories.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across different dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of multivariate functional time series forecasting accuracy using rolling window evaluation, compared to existing methods such as multivariate functional ARIMA and multiresidual MFSSA. Additionally, we provide MFSSA as a platform for further research and development in the field of multivariate functional time series.

This research study investigates the long-term behavior of a specific type of random walk model, focusing on the analysis of the probability of which a certain event occurs within a particular time frame. We examine two categories of models: one with a fixed starting point and the other without a fixed starting point. For the model without a fixed starting point, we consider a special case where the underlying process exhibits stationary properties. Our primary findings are that for the model with a fixed starting point, there are conditions under which the probability of which the event occurs within the given time frame converges to a steady-state probability at an exponential rate. Additionally, for the model without a fixed starting point, we find that this probability also converges to a steady-state probability at an exponential rate, and this result holds even in the absence of stationarity conditions. These results can be seen as extensions of previous research on the long-term behavior of random walk models, and they provide a new insight into the relationship between the shape of the underlying process and the ease with which it is possible to distinguish between different time periods.

A detailed study of the ICRF test facility IShTAR's plasma generator has been conducted, focusing on the helicon regime where a plasma current and magnetic field intersect at a right angle. To validate these findings, IShTAR's plasma parameters were matched to those of the helicon regime using discharge power in the range of 400-600 kW, resulting in plasma densities between 3.8x10^19 and 5.7x10^19 electrons per cubic meter at a temperature of 2.2 eV. This alignment enabled the successful operation of the helicon regime for up to 25 ms, and allowed for the reduction of plasma density by increasing the distance between the antenna and the plasma, as well as raising the antenna above the plasma axis. Furthermore, fluctuations in the plasma generator's helicon regime were examined, revealing that plasma densities remain stable deep within the plasma chamber, and that density fluctuations in the helicon regime are less severe than those found in the ohmic regime.

Nucleus segmentation in histopathology images is a critical step for automated disease diagnosis. To address the challenge of accurately identifying specific cell nuclei within complex tissue backgrounds, a novel dual-stage network called W-Net has been developed. This network comprises two reverse U-nets that operate in a series, where the output of the first U-net is used as input to drive the segmentation of all nuclei in the image. The resulting dataset is then combined with the original image to guide a second U-net focused on isolating the target nuclei. W-Net has been tested on datasets for brain and liver cancer diagnosis and has been compared to leading competing models, demonstrating its superior performance in both assessments.

Given a non-Archimedean local field, we define the regional converse theorem for a specific group G up to a scalar factor in terms of character automorphy factors. This determination enables us to state the regional converse theorem for the special orthogonal group SO_n(K) and the symplectic group Sp_2n(K) as equivalent statements to certain non-triviality conditions for specific symmetric and exterior power functions. We also establish that for these groups, the regional converse theorem holds when the underlying field has characteristic zero and allows algebraic closure.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a type of convolutional neural networks adapted to process complex, node-related data on graph structures and have been effectively applied in various tasks. However, the fundamental concept behind GCNNs, particularly graph convolution, remains unclear to many researchers. Multiple GCNN models exist, and they extend traditional convolutional neural networks in different ways, making their performance equivalent but without a clear understanding of why this performance is similar. In an attempt to address this uncertainty, we study the basic graph convolution function and discover that it corresponds to a specific type of filtered convolutional neural networks. This specific filter multiplies the input by a learned matrix of weights and correlates with a cosine function, providing a unique insight into graph convolution. We also examine three well-known GCNN models, finding that they all resemble filtered convolutional neural networks or combination of them. Our analysis demonstrates that the performance of these GCNN models is equivalent to traditional convolutional neural networks due to their ability to process data in a way that is similar to how traditional convolutional neural networks process data, thereby extending their functionality to graph structures without losing their fundamental characteristics. We make publicly available our code for the filtered GCNN models mentioned in this study.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, we demonstrate that a scalar field coupled to gravity, as described by a Chern-Simons action, leads to consistent and well-defined physics. This framework results in smooth, spinning soliton solutions and hairy black holes, even when the cosmological constant is positive. Furthermore, we show that linearized gravity within this context is directly linked to a specific scalar field Chern-Simons action, effectively mimicking the behavior of gravity through a proxy. This relationship is validated through the analysis of both soliton solutions and the oscillations of hairy black holes.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Nonetheless, the accuracy of this imaging method can be hindered by significant sources of error, particularly in cancer diagnosis. Notably, the estimation of liver cancer's lateral shift, which indicates the movement of tissues, poses a significant challenge for elastography systems. To address this challenge, a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method is proposed, utilizing a synthetic aperture technique that assumes a virtual origin. By optimizing the placement of sensors and using the coherence of the acquired signal, the VOSA method enhances the spatial resolution and reduces the estimation error of liver cancer's lateral shift. In simulations, the proposed algorithm demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, outperforming the conventional synthetic aperture technique by 85% in estimation error. Furthermore, the proposed method is applicable to various elastography systems, including elastography integrated in ultrasound scanners.

Our proposed method, “Rational Pseudocode,” is a new algorithmic approach that combines human-made code with human performances on a specific task, allowing for the efficient creation of compelling and explanatory models. Unlike traditional training methods that rely solely on performance data, Rational Pseudocode leverages a unique blend of expert code and performances to train a generative model, thereby unlocking the potential for human-made code to influence performance explanations. We have conducted a series of experiments covering simple mathematical problems, complex language models, and computer vision tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and the significant impact of incorporating human-made code into models. The resulting models are not only highly accurate but also prone to generating clear and intuitive explanations, as shown in Figure 1, which highlights exemplary models produced using Rational Pseudocode on various tasks.

In the context of high-dimensional data with a large number $n$ of points, where the dimensionality is represented by $d$, we develop a a a fast and efficient algorithm for the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution uses $n^{1-\epsilon}$ memory and completes in $poly(1/\epsilon, \delta, \phi)d^2n^3$ time, also enabling us to obtain a approximately optimal result within the same time frame. Additionally, we simplify and improve previous approaches for the static and semi-dynamic variants of the problem. Our results build upon the previous work of [CT20] and [CR20] which introduced the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem and the approximate centroid technique, and provide an $O(1)$ factor improvement over the previous time complexity for the semi-dynamic variant.

On a grid, we're looking at a game where an pursuer with perfect information is up against a flawless agent representing an evader without perfect vision. The pursuer's goal is to capture the evader within a pre-determined number of steps, while the evader aims to avoid being captured or reach a specific target in the grid. Since the game involves chance, we're treating it as a stochastic pursuit game. To break it down, we're dividing it into smaller parts called hierarchical divisions. Each hierarchical division represents a separate stochastic pursuit game. By converting these divisions into a tree format and assigning values to the leaves, we can use dynamic programming to find the value of each branch, effectively finding the value of the original game.

This work presents an efficient method for estimating the rapidity densities of weak bosons in high-energy muon collisions, with a particular focus on integrating various vector boson distributions in relation to lead-nucleus collisions. A novel approach is proposed to estimate the effects of multiple weak boson productions in such collisions. This estimation method leverages two parameters: the average number of weak bosons produced per event and the average number of weak bosons produced per unit rapidity length in collisions. This proposed method is utilized in a multiple weak boson production simulation, with results shown for various collisions. This estimation method levers simple, closed-form expressions to evaluate integral functions of weak boson distributions, significantly improving computation efficiency.

Reinforcement learning through model-driven multi-task training holds promise in producing highly versatile agents. By simultaneously completing a range of tasks, the agent develops a strong ability to adapt to new situations. Nonetheless, when introduced to unfamiliar tasks, the agent often experiences significant setbacks, negating the benefits of its versatile training. In response to this challenge, we develop a modular system for learning multiple tasks simultaneously. This system ensures that each module's learning remains relatively isolated, preventing widespread disruption when encountering unknown tasks. Our results demonstrate that this modular approach allows the agent to effectively navigate complex scenarios characterized by a mix of familiar and unfamiliar tasks. In one notable example, introducing a new task that differs from the existing ones by only 20% causes only a minor decline of 5% in the agent's performance. Our approach is applicable to a wide range of scenarios and demonstrates the efficacy of model-driven multi-task reinforcement learning in real-world situations.
We explore an interesting development involving logics, specifically within the framework of intuitionistic modal logic, where we investigate the gathering of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser.

This paper develops a three-spheres theorem for non-zero Dirac-helmholtz data G, where the underlying manifold is a compact, connected, smooth manifold M of dimension n>2. If G has minimal degree 2m+1, the theorem states that for a non-zero G, there exists exactly one (up to scalar multiplication) non-zero L2 solution f to the Dirac equation Df =0, satisfying the boundary condition af+G=0 for some non-zero function a on the (n-1)-sphere S^(n-1).

In inverse problems, the goal is to recover an original parameter given a distorted observation. Despite significant progress, solving inverse problems is often hindered by several constraints, including limited data, poor quality observations, or a combination of both, as well as multiple equally plausible solutions. To address these issues, a novel framework is proposed to utilize a regularized conditional Generative Adversarial Network (RCGAN) to recover both the sharp and accurate recovery of the underlying parameter and a reliability indicator to represent the credibility of each sample in the recovery. As the reliability indicator is obtained by training the network to predict the likelihood of each sample, given the observed data, it is modeled as a probability density function. To further reduce multiple equally plausible solutions to a single solution, we select the sample corresponding to the highest probability density as the final recovery result. Experimental evaluations of the proposed method on low-dose CT images and inverse problems with multiple solutions yielded reliable and consistent results, demonstrating the effectiveness of RCGAN for tackling real-world inverse challenges.

This study examines the possibility of surfaces being invariant within a specific class of dynamical systems that incorporate non-local feedback. We begin by reviewing the concept of invariant surfaces in traditional dynamical systems before adapting a specific technique from this context to tackle the scenario of dynamical systems with local and non-local feedback. This involves a $N$-dimensional state space with local feedback defined by $\dot{x} = A x + f(x)$ and a hyperball $B_\rho$ as its stable region. In contrast, the system with non-local feedback is represented by $\dot{x} = A x + f(\Lambda x)$, where $\Lambda$ denotes a diagonal scaling matrix. We demonstrate that certain conditions on the size of $\Lambda$ relative to the distance from the origin $\rho$ are sufficient to determine the absence of invariant surfaces within the system with non-local feedback.

The interstellar medium is capable of shaping its surrounding space with plasmas from expired stars, supernovae, and other energetic events. Pulsar scintillation patterns can serve as a valuable tool for mapping the behavior of the interstellar medium. Our observation of a strong scintillation pattern from the bright pulsar B1133+16 reveals a non-uniform distance to this pulsar of $1.16 \pm 0.03$ kpc, indicating that the pulsar lies within a distant stellar association that includes the Cassiopeia Nebula. This association has not been observed in the infrared spectrum since it lacks a prominent signature, although it does exhibit a gradual temperature increase. Further research is necessary to confirm these findings, but they also hint at the possibility of investigating other similar phenomena.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to time-dependent patterns by employing dynamic dilated convolution layers that change based on estimated signal period lengths. Secondly, a cascade connection is introduced to integrate external signal components in the frequency domain into the model, enabling the network to incorporate prior knowledge. Evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the effectiveness of both proposed modules for modeling periodic signals and the framework's superiority over WN in terms of log-likelihood scores and subjective quality assessments.

Bicategories incorporate bicategory morphisms, extending category theory principles to a higher level of complexity. Building on the concept of marks introduced by Baez, Berman, and Tobias, we establish a connection between shadows and bicategory morphisms. Specifically, we show that the image of a mark under a bicategory morphism is the shadow of its corresponding mark under a particular bicategory morphism, dubbed the shadow functor. This relationship serves as the foundation for interpreting the image of a mark as its shadow.

For individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, obtaining visual information from audio sources like police sirens, fire alarms, or doorbell sounds can be critical for ensuring safety and accessibility. However, these sounds are frequently difficult to locate due to the background noise levels present in environments like public transportation, homes, or public spaces. To address this issue, we propose a method for estimating the origin of auditory sounds that are semiautomatic and efficient. This approach leverages a limited set of short-time audio recordings from specific locations and combines a custom feature extraction method with a spatial-aware model. We evaluate our proposed technique using audio recordings from 13 diverse locations with low frequency bands, and our results show that it is possible to accurately predict sound sources on maps by assigning a probability distribution based on spatial coordinates. Moreover, our analysis reveals correlations between sound sources and spatial features in various environments. Finally, we outline potential pathways for transitioning from sound source localization to visual information retrieval, enabling access to visual data superimposed on real-time maps via video streams or VR headsets.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the massive amount of data being generated and the importance of distance-based relationships in GNNs discussed in the literature. The impact of network geometry on GNN performance has been supported by both theoretical and experimental evidence. Despite this progress, existing GNN models fail to utilize a fundamental property of geometric distances, namely the property of being positive definite. This limitation leads to the undesirable effect where the loss function value can become negative, which is not a geometric distance. To address this issue, we propose a novel GNN model called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN). LGNN operates in a geometric space where distances are computed using the Lorentzian norm, which enables our model to prevent negative loss function values. Furthermore, we prove that LGNN maintains several significant properties that are advantageous for modeling complex data, including non-singularity, positive definiteness, and the ability to compute accurate geometric distances. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we conducted a series of experiments across multiple categories, including classification, reconstruction, and generation, which showed that LGNN outperforms existing GNN baselines in nearly all cases. The code for LGNN is now available online.

Reconstructing sources that generate waves in a structured environment with multiple boundaries can be extremely challenging, especially when there are reflections causing confusion. This research involves identifying an unknown sound-producing area within a complex structure containing several boundaries, using measurements of waves in the air. By assuming the source is a single point, we used an iterative reconstruction method to determine its location and characteristics. However, achieving accurate results proved difficult, mainly due to misinterpretation of wave reflections. Nonetheless, we observed that precise coordination between sound waves and the structured environment is crucial for successful source identification.

This study makes novel exponential delay models with deviations from the usual exponential behavior available for predictive purposes. It also extends the framework to include fractional powers of the usual exponential function, offering a robust and versatile model that can be utilized across various contexts, such as financial analysis, biology, chemistry, physics, and medicine. Notably, this research provides a specific example of applying the model to analyze stock price patterns.

We investigate the harmonic gauge choice in a theory with an arbitrarily small speed of light. Under certain conditions, including access to high-resolution metrics, we provide nonlinear harmonic gauge choices that ensure symmetry preservation and stability. Interestingly, a specific linear harmonic gauge that ensures symmetry preservation does not require a minimum resolution. We also examine the effects of a cosmological constant within the framework of Einstein's gravity and show that it impairs the stability of the gauge.

Weyl-Wigner formalism provides a graphical phase space representation of quantum operators, with Weyl symbols serving as the basis for a positive definite matrix-valued function. This formalism allows for the visualization of Poisson brackets in the phase space, directly relating to commutators in the Hilbert space. By utilizing a basis of Weyl operators, a set of canonical thermal equilibrium conditions can be visually depicted through a set of integral equations in phase space. Solving these equations yields a explicit solution for the Weyl symbols of thermal equilibrium operators, with a notable finding that they correspond to classical Gaussian distributions in the phase space. This result is further verified by comparing it to existing solutions obtained via other methods.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been understood for nearly a century, since the work of Bloch in 1933, and has found applications in both classical and quantum systems. We review the fundamental principles that lead to this concept, then examine the types of quantum systems that have been found to exhibit negative temperature, including autonomous systems, systems in equilibrium, and open systems. We discuss the relation between negative temperature and system properties such as entropy, fluctuations, and chemical potential. Finally, we explore the promise held by negative absolute temperatures to increase the efficiency of physical processes and enhance the duration of periodic system variations.

We have developed an easy scoto-seesaw framework, which incorporates both neutrino mass generation and dark matter physics, while also addressing the Higgs vacuum stability issue. Within this framework, we can utilize natural and minimal natural neutrino parameters and assume the existence of a heavy dark sector. Here, we focus on the minimal version of the framework, where one generation of dark matter interacts with one neutrino species. Furthermore, we have established that the ease scoto-seesaw framework meets all required conditions, including successful neutrino mass generation, dark matter stability and consistency with terrestrial and celestial observations, the electroweak symmetry breaking, and the stability of the Higgs vacuum. Additionally, we found that the ease scoto-seesaw framework exhibits notable similarities with the inverse and normal fermion Yukawa vacuum stability scenarios. Moreover, we have explored the potential for vacuum stability in the ease scoto-seesaw framework and identified potential robustness issues with the minimal version. However, we have also demonstrated that this issue can be resolved by introducing additional fermion degrees of freedom, both light and heavy, which not only address the vacuum stability but may also impact neutrino mass parameters and dark matter phenomenology.

We use a one-band Hubbard model to investigate the orbitally degenerate $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ $d$-electron case, varying the ratio of on-site Hubbard interaction to bandwidth and spin-orbit coupling. Calculations are performed numerically using a exact diagonalization method for a honeycomb lattice with nearest and next-nearest neighbor interactions. Our results show that the one-band and multi-band descriptions converge in favor of a one-band model in large enough bands, across different on-site couplings and lattices. The interplay of on-site interaction and spin-orbit coupling leads to a varying degree of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, ultimately producing an energy spectrum that can be understood using a multi-band perspective. Nevertheless, the one-band model retains its relevance and accurately captures the low-energy physics, even when the bands are wide. Consequently, we expect it to be a suitable choice for incorporating the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in effective one-band models for, e.g., $d^1$ and $d^2$ fillings within 4d and 5d transition metal compounds.

This research examines how changes in a diagram influence relative Lagrangian submodules and, by extension, the associated invariants. Specifically, we examine even-dimensional Lagrangian submodules and their corresponding measures within a specific homological context. To achieve this, we analyze the effects of certain diagram transformations on these measures and their measures under a change of variables. Furthermore, we establish relationships between these measures and certain invariants derived from a particular mathematical construction. These relationships can be used to pair certain elements of the homological context. Additionally, we explore a particular case involving a specific diagram and its associated measures, including a computational approach to calculating these measures. This research is motivated by the connection to certain topological invariants, specifically the extended Chern-Simons functional, and involves a collaboration with D. Karpushin.

Chest X-rays are a widely used diagnostic tool with a broad range of applications, from identifying respiratory conditions like pneumonia to detecting cardiovascular disease. However, interpreting X-rays also carries the risk of misinformation and false narratives being spread quickly. In this paper, we examine the challenges of fact-checking X-rays on social media platforms. We focus on verifying claims related to COVID-19, but our approach is versatile enough to extend to other illnesses. To achieve this, we propose a straightforward yet effective method for validating X-ray-based statements. It involves utilizing a simple neural network to classify normal and abnormal chest X-rays, and a more complex ensemble model to classify X-rays featuring specific symptoms. We also introduce a new dataset consisting of 5,000 labeled X-ray images, along with 2,000 text-based statements claiming the presence of COVID-19. In addition to benchmarking our ensemble model on this dataset, we explore ways to enhance reliability by reducing false positives and investigating the possibility of training on publicly accessible X-ray images. Our code and dataset are available for download at the following URLs: https://github.com/ghaneee/CXF and https://github.com/ghaneee/CXF-Dataset.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization, consisting of three primary views: a lower section displaying vector plots, a middle section with a time curve, and an upper section showing a variety of other plots. The application can generate a range of plots including scatter plots, phase plots, gel plots, trilinear plots, and circle plots. ViDaExpert is designed to accommodate large datasets and includes an automated analysis feature that generates reports on dataset characteristics. The application can also read output from MFA, SVD, and PCA analyses.
